questions.stem: A homogeneous mixture whose composition is uniform at the molecular scale is called a
options: compound with fixed mass ratio only
questions.explanation: A solution is a single-phase homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent.

questions.stem: Ordinary air is best classified as a solution of the type
questions.explanation: Nitrogen, oxygen and the other constituents form a gaseous solution.

questions.stem: Brass (copper plus zinc) is a textbook example of a
questions.explanation: Alloys such as brass are solid solutions of metals in metals.

questions.stem: Solubility of a solid in a liquid is the largest amount that dissolves to give a
options: saturated solution at the stated temperature
questions.explanation: The saturated composition at that temperature is the solubility.

questions.stem: Raising the external pressure over a liquid changes the solubility most for a
questions.explanation: Gas solubility is strongly pressure-dependent; solids and liquids are almost unaffected.

questions.stem: Hydrogen taken up by palladium metal is classified as a
questions.explanation: H2/Pd is the usual Intermediate example of a gas dissolved in a solid.

questions.stem: Undissolved crystals remaining in contact with a solution at equilibrium show that the solution is
questions.explanation: Saturation is the equilibrium state with excess undissolved solute present.

questions.stem: Ethanol and water dissolve in each other in every proportion, so they are
questions.explanation: Complete miscibility means a single liquid phase at all compositions.

questions.stem: Most ionic solids dissolve in water endothermically. Warming a saturated sample of such a salt typically
options: converts the salt into a gas
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier’s principle: heat is a reactant for endothermic dissolution, so solubility rises with T.

questions.stem: Oxygen is poorer in warm pond water than in cold water because dissolving a gas is usually
options: exothermic, so heating drives gas out
endothermic, so heating pulls gas in
questions.explanation: Gas dissolution releases heat; raising T lowers the equilibrium solubility.

questions.stem: A cooled solution that still holds more solute than the equilibrium value at that temperature is
questions.explanation: Supersaturation is a metastable state above the equilibrium solubility.

questions.stem: The rule “like dissolves like” predicts that molecular iodine dissolves readily in
questions.explanation: I2 is non-polar and is far more soluble in CCl4 than in water.

questions.stem: Dental and laboratory amalgams are solutions in which the solvent is
questions.explanation: An amalgam is a metal (or metals) dissolved in mercury.

questions.stem: A sealed soda is opened and then left in the sun. CO2 escapes more freely because
options: both the pressure drop and the temperature rise lower gas solubility
only the pressure change matters; heat raises gas solubility
heating alone increases the Henry solubility
solids and gases respond identically to pressure
questions.explanation: Henry’s law: less partial pressure means less dissolved gas, and warming further decreases gas solubility.

questions.stem: Mass percent of a dissolved substance is 100 times the ratio of
options: mass of solute to mass of solution
moles of solute to litres of solution
moles of solute to kilograms of solvent
volume of solute to volume of solvent
questions.explanation: w/w % = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100.

questions.stem: Mole fraction of component A in a binary mixture equals
options: mass of A / mass of B
questions.explanation: Mole fraction is the mole share of that component among all moles present.

questions.stem: Molarity counts the moles of solute present in
questions.explanation: M = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres.

questions.stem: Molality places in the denominator the
options: mass of the whole solution in grams
questions.explanation: m = moles of solute / kilograms of solvent, so it is independent of solution volume.

questions.stem: Parts per million by mass is defined as
options: $10^6$ times (mass of solute / mass of solution)
$10^3$ times (mass of solute / mass of solution)
moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
questions.explanation: ppm (w/w) = $10^6 \times w_{\mathrm{solute}} / w_{\mathrm{solution}}$.

questions.stem: Among the usual concentration units, the one that does not shift when the solution is warmed is
questions.explanation: Molality uses solvent mass, which does not expand with temperature; molarity uses volume.

questions.stem: Adding the mole fractions of every component of a solution yields
questions.explanation: Mole fractions are fractions of a whole, so $\sum x_i = 1$.

questions.stem: Volume percent is the concentration unit most often quoted for
questions.explanation: v/v % is convenient when both solute and solvent are liquids.

questions.stem: A 1.0 molal aqueous preparation contains 1.0 mol of solute dissolved in
questions.explanation: Molality is moles per kilogram of solvent, not per litre of solution.

questions.stem: Mass/volume percent is 100 times the ratio of
options: mass of solute to volume of solution
volume of solute to mass of solvent
moles of solute to kilograms of solvent
mass of solvent to mass of solute
questions.explanation: w/v % = (mass of solute / volume of solution) × 100, with consistent units.

questions.stem: For a very dilute aqueous sample, 1 ppm is nearly the same as
options: 1 mg of solute in one litre of solution
questions.explanation: 1 L of dilute aqueous solution has a mass of about 10³ g, so 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg L⁻¹.

questions.stem: Molarity of a sealed bottle of solution falls slightly on heating because
questions.explanation: Thermal expansion increases V while n stays fixed, so M = n/V drops.

questions.stem: Normality of a solution is the number of
options: gram equivalents of solute in one litre of solution
moles of solute in one kilogram of solvent
questions.explanation: N = gram equivalents of solute / litres of solution.

questions.stem: Mole fraction is a concentration that is
questions.explanation: It is a pure number — a ratio of moles to moles.

questions.stem: A student dissolves 10 g of NaOH in 90 g of water. The mass percent of NaOH is
questions.explanation: Mass of solution = 100 g, so w/w % = 10/100 × 100 = 10%.

questions.stem: Two moles of ethanol are mixed with three moles of water. Mole fraction of ethanol is
4.9 g of H2SO4 (98 g mol⁻¹) made up to 500 mL of solution has molarity
questions.explanation: Moles = 4.9/98 = 0.050; volume = 0.50 L, so M = 0.10 mol L⁻¹.

questions.stem: Dissolving 6.0 g of urea (60 g mol⁻¹) in 250 g of water produces molality
questions.explanation: Moles of urea = 0.10; kilograms of water = 0.250, so m = 0.40 mol kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: A 100 ppm aqueous impurity corresponds, in 1.0 kg of solution, to a solute mass of
Glucose (180 g mol⁻¹), 9.0 g, sits together with 81 g of water. Mole fraction of glucose is nearest
An aqueous bottle labelled 2.0 M NaCl occupies 250 mL. Moles of NaCl inside are
questions.explanation: n = M V = 2.0 mol L⁻¹ × 0.250 L = 0.50 mol.

questions.stem: Aqueous HCl is 36.5% (w/w) with density 1.18 g mL⁻¹. Using molar mass 36.5 g mol⁻¹, the molarity is nearest
questions.explanation: One litre has mass 1180 g and contains 0.365 × 1180 = 431 g HCl, i.e. 11.8 mol, so M ≈ 11.8.

questions.stem: A flask holds 8.0 g of CH3OH (32 g mol⁻¹) plus 36 g of water. Molality of methanol is nearest
questions.explanation: n(CH3OH) = 0.25 mol in 0.036 kg of water, so m = 0.25/0.036 ≈ 6.9 mol kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: Mixing 200 mL of 0.60 M H2SO4 with 300 mL of 0.20 M H2SO4, taking volumes as additive, gives a blend of
Henry linked the partial pressure of a dissolved gas to its
questions.explanation: One form is $p = K_H x$, with x the mole fraction of the dissolved gas.

questions.stem: The Henry-law constant $K_H$ is dimensionally a
questions.explanation: Because $p = K_H x$ and x is dimensionless, $K_H$ has the unit of pressure.

questions.stem: At a fixed temperature, a larger $K_H$ for a gas means that gas is
options: exactly as soluble as every other gas
questions.explanation: x = p / $K_H$, so a large constant implies a small dissolved mole fraction.

questions.stem: Soft-drink bottles are packed under extra carbon-dioxide pressure so that
options: more CO2 remains dissolved until the cap is opened
the drink freezes in the bottle
questions.explanation: Higher p(CO2) forces a larger x(CO2) in the liquid (Henry’s law).

questions.stem: Deep-sea divers risk decompression sickness because nitrogen
options: dissolves more at high pressure and bubbles out on a rapid ascent
forms an azeotrope with blood plasma
questions.explanation: High p(N2) loads the blood; a sudden drop in pressure releases bubbles in the tissues.

questions.stem: Warming a solvent generally
questions.explanation: Gas dissolution is exothermic, so $K_H$ increases and x falls as T rises.

questions.stem: A compact statement of Henry’s law for a sparingly soluble gas is
questions.explanation: Partial pressure of the gas is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.

questions.stem: At 298 K, $K_H$ for N2 in water is 8.0 × 10⁴ atm. Under 0.80 atm of nitrogen the dissolved mole fraction is
Two gases have $K_H$ values 2 × 10³ atm and 5 × 10⁴ atm. At the same partial pressure the more soluble gas is the one with
questions.explanation: Solubility falls as $K_H$ rises, so the smaller constant marks the more soluble gas.

questions.stem: A mountaineer takes up less oxygen at high altitude mainly because
options: the partial pressure of O2 in the air is lower
nitrogen is absent from the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Henry’s law: dissolved x(O2) tracks p(O2), which falls as total air pressure falls.

questions.stem: If the partial pressure of CO2 above a drink is doubled at constant temperature, the dissolved mole fraction of CO2
questions.explanation: x ∝ p at fixed T, so doubling p doubles the dissolved mole fraction.

questions.stem: Dry air is 0.21 mole fraction oxygen. With $K_H$(O2) = 3.3 × 10⁷ torr and a total air pressure of 760 torr, dissolved x(O2) is nearest
For volatile component A in an ideal liquid mixture, Raoult’s relation is written
questions.explanation: Partial pressure equals the pure-liquid vapour pressure times the liquid mole fraction.

questions.stem: Total vapour pressure over an ideal binary liquid equals
questions.explanation: Each component contributes independently: $p_{\mathrm{total}} = \sum p_i^\circ x_i$.

questions.stem: Dissolving a non-volatile solute in a pure solvent
questions.explanation: Solvent mole fraction falls below 1, so $p = p^\circ x_{\mathrm{solvent}} < p^\circ$.

questions.stem: Vapour in equilibrium with an ideal A–B liquid is richer in the component that has the
questions.explanation: The more volatile liquid (larger $p^\circ$) contributes a larger partial pressure, so $y > x$ for that component.

questions.stem: A graph of total vapour pressure against liquid mole fraction for an ideal binary pair is
questions.explanation: Ideal $p_{\mathrm{total}}$ varies linearly between the two pure-liquid vapour pressures.

questions.stem: Dalton’s law applied to the vapour above a solution gives the vapour mole fraction of A as
questions.explanation: Each partial pressure is that component’s mole fraction in the gas times the total pressure.

questions.stem: Raoult’s law for the solvent becomes exact in the limit of a solution that is
questions.explanation: The solvent then has $x \approx 1$ and behaves as a nearly pure liquid obeying Raoult’s law.

questions.stem: A closed flask of pure liquid A at equilibrium exerts
questions.explanation: The equilibrium vapour pressure of the pure liquid is the $p^\circ$ used in Raoult’s law.

questions.stem: When the liquid is pure A ($x_A = 1$), Raoult’s law reduces to
questions.explanation: The partial pressure of a pure liquid is just its own vapour pressure.

questions.stem: Two liquids that obey Raoult’s law at every composition are said to form
questions.explanation: Ideal solutions follow $p_i = p_i^\circ x_i$ over the whole composition range.

questions.stem: A clear drop in vapour pressure is used as a colligative effect when the added solute is
options: non-volatile (or far less volatile than the solvent)
questions.explanation: Only then does the total pressure fall below $p^\circ$ of the pure solvent.

questions.stem: For an ideal mix the vapour mole fraction of A is related to the liquid composition by
questions.explanation: Combine Raoult ($p_A = p_A^\circ x_A$) with Dalton ($y_A = p_A / p_{\mathrm{total}}$).

questions.stem: At a given temperature, the liquid with the larger $p^\circ$ is described as
questions.explanation: Volatility tracks the equilibrium vapour pressure of the pure liquid.

questions.stem: Pure toluene has vapour pressure 30 torr. In an ideal mix with $x_{\mathrm{toluene}} = 0.40$, the partial pressure of toluene is
questions.explanation: $p = p^\circ x = 30 \times 0.40 = 12$ torr.

questions.stem: An ideal pair has $p_A^\circ = 80$ mm Hg and $p_B^\circ = 20$ mm Hg. At $x_A = 0.50$ the total pressure is
questions.explanation: $p = 80 \times 0.50 + 20 \times 0.50 = 50$ mm Hg.

questions.stem: Benzene ($p^\circ = 75$ torr) plus a non-volatile solute form a liquid with $x_{\mathrm{benzene}} = 0.90$. The vapour pressure of that solution is
questions.explanation: Only benzene contributes: $p = 75 \times 0.90 = 67.5$ torr.

questions.stem: Above an ideal liquid the partial pressure of A is 24 kPa while the total pressure is 60 kPa. The vapour mole fraction of A is
questions.explanation: $y_A = p_A / p_{\mathrm{total}} = 24/60 = 0.40$.

questions.stem: Component B is non-volatile. If $x_{\mathrm{solvent}} = 0.95$ and $p^\circ_{\mathrm{solvent}} = 20$ kPa, the solution vapour pressure equals
Two ideal liquids are present in equal mole fractions. $p_A^\circ = 90$ torr and $p_B^\circ = 60$ torr. Total vapour pressure is
questions.explanation: $p = 0.50 \times 90 + 0.50 \times 60 = 75$ torr.

questions.stem: Vapour over an ideal mix is analysed as $y_A = 0.70$ when $p_{\mathrm{total}} = 100$ torr. Partial pressure of A in that vapour is
questions.explanation: $p_A = y_A p_{\mathrm{total}} = 0.70 \times 100 = 70$ torr.

questions.stem: An ideal blend has $x_A = 0.30$, $p_A^\circ = 200$ torr and $p_B^\circ = 100$ torr. Mole fraction of A in the vapour is nearest
questions.explanation: $p_A = 60$ torr, $p_B = 70$ torr, $p = 130$ torr, so $y_A = 60/130 \approx 0.46$.

questions.stem: At 350 K the liquid mole fraction of hexane is 0.25 ($p^\circ_{\mathrm{hex}} = 90$ kPa, $p^\circ_{\mathrm{hept}} = 30$ kPa). Total vapour pressure of this ideal pair is
An ideal liquid solution is characterised by
questions.explanation: No heat is absorbed or evolved and the volumes are strictly additive for an ideal mix.

questions.stem: Molecular interactions in an ideal A–B solution satisfy
options: A–A, B–B and A–B forces of similar strength
A–B much stronger than like pairs
A–B much weaker than like pairs
questions.explanation: Equal interaction energies make the mixture obey Raoult’s law at all compositions.

questions.stem: Benzene and toluene form a nearly ideal pair because they have
options: hydrogen bonds of very different strength
questions.explanation: Both are non-polar aromatics of comparable size, so A–B forces match A–A and B–B.

questions.stem: A non-ideal solution is one that
options: obeys Raoult’s law at every mole fraction
questions.explanation: Any measurable departure of vapour pressure from $p_i^\circ x_i$ marks non-ideality.

questions.stem: Positive deviation from Raoult’s law means the observed vapour pressure is
questions.explanation: Weaker A–B forces let molecules escape more easily, so $p > p_{\mathrm{ideal}}$.

questions.stem: Negative deviation from Raoult’s law is accompanied by
questions.explanation: Stronger A–B attractions release heat on mixing (exothermic).

questions.stem: For a positively deviating pair, mixing typically causes the volume to
questions.explanation: Weaker unlike attractions leave a slightly expanded, less tightly packed liquid.

questions.stem: Chloroform and acetone show negative deviation because
options: a hydrogen-bond-like attraction forms between the two molecules
questions.explanation: The chloroform hydrogen interacts with the acetone oxygen, strengthening A–B forces.

questions.stem: Ethanol–acetone is a common Intermediate example of
questions.explanation: Mixing breaks some ethanol hydrogen bonds, so A–B is weaker than A–A and the pair shows positive deviation.

questions.stem: n-Hexane and n-heptane are expected to behave as
questions.explanation: Adjacent homologues have nearly identical London forces, so the mix is essentially ideal.

questions.stem: When A–B attractions are weaker than A–A and B–B, the mixture shows
options: positive deviation and often a minimum-boiling azeotrope
negative deviation and a maximum-boiling azeotrope
questions.explanation: Weaker unlike forces raise vapour pressure; a maximum in p versus x gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope.

questions.stem: Nitric acid and water mix with heat released and a vapour-pressure curve below the Raoult line. The deviation is
questions.explanation: Exothermic mixing plus $p < p_{\mathrm{ideal}}$ is the signature of negative deviation.

questions.stem: Carbon disulphide and acetone form a pair with weaker unlike interactions, so one expects
questions.explanation: CS2–acetone is a standard positively deviating pair.

questions.stem: For an ideal solution the plot of $p_A$ versus $x_A$ is
questions.explanation: Raoult’s law $p_A = p_A^\circ x_A$ is a straight line through the origin and $(1, p_A^\circ)$.

questions.stem: A liquid pair with $\Delta V_{\mathrm{mix}}$ negative and $p$ below the ideal line is classified as
questions.explanation: Volume contraction and lowered vapour pressure both point to stronger A–B attractions.

questions.stem: A binary liquid shows $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mix}}$ negative and total vapour pressure below the Raoult prediction at every composition. Distillation of this pair commonly yields
options: an ideal vapour of unchanged composition
questions.explanation: Negative deviation produces a minimum in p versus x and therefore a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

questions.stem: Colligative properties of a dilute solution depend on
options: the number of solute particles, not their chemical identity
the charge of the solute only
questions.explanation: Particle count (mole fraction or molality) fixes the size of a colligative effect for a given solvent.

questions.stem: Relative lowering of vapour pressure is defined as
questions.explanation: It is the fractional drop in solvent vapour pressure caused by the solute.

questions.stem: For a dilute solution of a non-volatile non-electrolyte, $(p^\circ - p) / p^\circ$ equals
options: the mole fraction of the solute
questions.explanation: Raoult’s law gives $(p^\circ - p)/p^\circ = x_{\mathrm{solute}}$ in the dilute non-volatile limit.

questions.stem: The four classical colligative properties include relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and
questions.explanation: Those four effects depend on the number of solute particles, not on their nature.

questions.stem: Relative lowering of vapour pressure does not depend on
options: the chemical identity of a non-electrolyte solute
the mole fraction of that solute
the vapour pressure of the pure solvent
whether the solute is present at all
questions.explanation: Any non-volatile non-electrolyte at the same $x_B$ produces the same relative lowering.

questions.stem: A non-volatile solute reduces vapour pressure because
options: the mole fraction of solvent molecules at the surface falls
the solute evaporates faster than the solvent
questions.explanation: Fewer solvent molecules occupy the surface, so the escape rate into the vapour falls.

questions.stem: In the dilute limit the vapour pressure of a solution of a non-volatile solute is $p^\circ$ multiplied by
options: the mole fraction of the solvent
the mole fraction of the solute
questions.explanation: $p = p^\circ x_{\mathrm{solvent}}$ is Raoult’s law for the solvent.

questions.stem: The molar mass of a non-volatile solute can be estimated from a measurement of
options: the density of the pure solute alone
questions.explanation: $(p^\circ - p)/p^\circ = n_B / (n_A + n_B)$ can be solved for $M_B$.

questions.stem: The Ostwald–Walker dynamic method is a classical experiment for measuring
questions.explanation: Air is passed through solution and then through pure solvent; the mass losses give $(p^\circ - p)/p^\circ$.

questions.stem: Two dilute solutions that share the same mole fraction of non-electrolyte solute in the same solvent show
options: different relative lowerings proportional to solute mass only
questions.explanation: Relative lowering tracks $x_B$, which is identical for the two solutions.

questions.stem: A solvent has $p^\circ = 80$ torr. After a non-volatile solute is added the pressure is 76 torr. Relative lowering is
Relative lowering of 0.020 is recorded for a dilute non-electrolyte. The mole fraction of solute is
questions.explanation: For a dilute non-volatile non-electrolyte, $(p^\circ - p)/p^\circ = x_B$.

questions.stem: Water (18 g mol⁻¹), 180 g, holds 6.0 g of a non-volatile solute. If relative lowering is 0.010, the molar mass of the solute is nearest
questions.explanation: n(water) = 10 mol; $x_B \approx n_B / n_A = 0.010$ gives $n_B = 0.10$ mol, so $M = 6.0 / 0.10 = 60$ g mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Pure solvent vapour pressure 50 kPa falls to 49 kPa on adding a non-volatile solute. The mole fraction of solvent is
questions.explanation: $x_{\mathrm{solvent}} = p / p^\circ = 49/50 = 0.98$.

questions.stem: Urea and glucose solutions that are equimolal in the same solvent exhibit
options: equal relative lowering, both being non-electrolytes
urea twice the lowering of glucose
questions.explanation: Equal molality in a dilute aqueous pair means essentially equal $x_B$ and therefore equal $(p^\circ - p)/p^\circ$.

questions.stem: A flask contains 3.0 g of a non-volatile solute ($M = 60$) together with 117 g of a solvent ($M = 78$). Relative lowering of vapour pressure is nearest
A non-volatile solute causes the boiling point of a liquid to
questions.explanation: The solution must be hotter before its vapour pressure reaches the external pressure.

questions.stem: The molal boiling-point elevation constant $K_b$ is also called the
questions.explanation: $K_b$ is the ebullioscopic (boiling-point) constant of the solvent.

questions.stem: $\Delta T_b$ for a dilute non-electrolyte solution is proportional to
options: the mole fraction of solvent only
questions.explanation: The working relation is $\Delta T_b = K_b m$.

questions.stem: $K_b$ is a characteristic of
options: the chemical identity of the solute
questions.explanation: Each solvent has its own molal elevation constant, independent of the non-electrolyte used.

questions.stem: Boiling point rises because the solution must be heated until its
options: vapour pressure again equals the external pressure
questions.explanation: A non-volatile solute lowers p, so a higher T is needed to restore p = 1 atm.

questions.stem: A convenient unit of $K_b$ is
questions.explanation: $\Delta T_b = K_b m$ with m in mol kg⁻¹, so $K_b$ has unit K kg mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: For water, the usual textbook $K_b$ is about
questions.explanation: The ebullioscopic constant of water is 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹ (often rounded to 0.52).

questions.stem: Molar mass of a non-volatile solute follows from $\Delta T_b$ if one also knows
options: only the colour of the solution
questions.explanation: $m = \Delta T_b / K_b$ and $m = (w_B / M_B) / w_A$ together give $M_B$.

questions.stem: Elevation of boiling point is classified as a
questions.explanation: It depends on the number of solute particles, not on their identity (for a non-electrolyte).

questions.stem: Between two dilute aqueous non-electrolytes, the larger boiling-point elevation belongs to the solution of
questions.explanation: $\Delta T_b = K_b m$ with the same $K_b$ (water), so the more molal solution boils higher.

questions.stem: A 1 molal aqueous non-electrolyte, taking $K_b = 0.52$ K kg mol⁻¹, is expected to boil near
questions.explanation: $\Delta T_b = 0.52$ K, so the boiling point is about 100.52 °C at 1 atm.

questions.explanation: $\Delta T_b$ scales directly with $K_b$ at fixed molality.

questions.explanation: n = 0.050 mol in 0.200 kg, so m = 0.25 mol kg⁻¹ and $\Delta T_b = 2.5 \times 0.25 = 0.625$ K.

questions.explanation: $\Delta T_b = i K_b m = 2 \times 0.52 \times 0.10 = 0.104$ K.

Adding a non-volatile solute to a solvent
questions.explanation: The solid solvent is in equilibrium with a solution of lower chemical potential, so the freezing point falls.

questions.stem: The molal freezing-point depression constant $K_f$ is also called the
questions.explanation: $K_f$ is the cryoscopic constant of the solvent.

questions.stem: $\Delta T_f$ for a dilute non-electrolyte equals
questions.explanation: The working relation is $\Delta T_f = K_f m$.

questions.stem: Antifreeze in a car radiator works by
options: depressing the freezing point of water
increasing the vapour pressure of ice
questions.explanation: Ethylene glycol is a non-volatile solute that lowers the freezing point of the coolant.

questions.stem: $K_f$ of water is about
questions.explanation: The cryoscopic constant of water is 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Freezing-point depression is a
questions.explanation: It depends on the number of solute particles in a given amount of solvent.

questions.stem: At the freezing point of a dilute solution, the solid that separates is generally
options: ice that contains all the solute
questions.explanation: The solute stays in the liquid; the first solid is almost always the pure solvent.

questions.stem: A larger $K_f$ at the same molality produces
questions.explanation: $\Delta T_f$ scales with $K_f$ when m is fixed.

questions.stem: Common salt is scattered on icy roads because NaCl
options: lowers the melting point of ice
raises the boiling point of ice
questions.explanation: Dissolved ions depress the freezing point, so ice melts at the ambient winter temperature.

questions.stem: The unit of $K_f$ is
questions.explanation: The same dimensions as $K_b$: temperature over molality.

questions.stem: Camphor is a popular cryoscopic solvent because it has
questions.explanation: A large cryoscopic constant magnifies $\Delta T_f$ and makes molar-mass measurements easier.

questions.explanation: n = 0.20 mol in 0.200 kg, so m = 1.0 mol kg⁻¹ and $\Delta T_f = 1.86$ K.

questions.stem: A solute (M = 128 g mol⁻¹), 6.4 g, in 100 g of a solvent ($K_f = 5.0$ K kg mol⁻¹) depresses the freezing point by
questions.explanation: n = 0.050 mol in 0.100 kg, so m = 0.50 mol kg⁻¹ and $\Delta T_f = 5.0 \times 0.50 = 2.5$ K.

questions.stem: A 0.050 m AlCl3 solution, taken as fully split (i = 4) in water ($K_f = 1.86$ K kg mol⁻¹), has $\Delta T_f$ nearest
